title: SQL UNION Operator
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behaviour of SQL UNION Operator.
Write valid SQLite queries that demonstrate the topic or a documented equivalent.
Predict result rows using the supplied sample data.
Identify common mistakes and important NULL or duplicate behaviour.
Choose an appropriate query pattern for a practical reporting task.

understand.concept: UNION combines the result rows of two or more SELECT statements and removes duplicate rows from the combined result. Each SELECT must return the same number of columns in compatible positions. Column names in the combined result are taken from the first SELECT.
understand.whyItMatters: UNION is useful when the same kind of record is stored in separate tables or query branches, such as current and archived customers or sales from different periods.
understand.analogy: Think of a database report as carefully combining or grouping rows from well-labelled registers to answer a specific question.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy does not model SQL's exact evaluation rules, duplicate semantics, three-valued NULL logic or dialect-specific features.

examples.title: Combine customer names without duplicates
examples.explanation: UNION removes duplicate result rows, so Asha appears once.

examples.title: Combine city lists without duplicates
examples.explanation: The result is a distinct set of cities from both periods.

examples.title: Combine aligned customer and city columns
examples.expectedOutput: Asha | Rajahmundry; Bilal | Hyderabad; Chitra | Vijayawada; Dev | Mumbai; Esha | Hyderabad
examples.explanation: Both SELECT statements return two compatible columns in the same order. The repeated Asha-city pair is removed.

examples.title: Combine filtered rows from both sources
examples.explanation: Each SELECT can apply its own WHERE condition before the result sets are combined.

examples.title: Use UNION to create a combined reporting set
examples.expectedOutput: 2025 | Asha; 2025 | Bilal; 2025 | Chitra; 2026 | Asha; 2026 | Dev; 2026 | Esha
examples.explanation: The year literal makes rows from different sources distinguishable, so the two Asha records are not duplicates.

practise.guidedTask: Run the setup, execute each SELECT separately, then combine them with UNION. Predict which complete rows are duplicates before running the combined query.
practise.independentTask: Create current_members and former_members tables with member_id, full_name and city. Write five UNION queries that combine names, cities and aligned two-column reports. Include one filtered branch and explain why duplicate removal happens on the entire selected row.
hints: Both SELECT branches must return the same number of columns.
Align columns by meaning and position, not just by name.
The combined output column names come from the first SELECT.
UNION removes duplicate complete rows, not just duplicates in one chosen column.
Use ORDER BY after the final SELECT to sort the combined result.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of SQL UNION Operator?
options: UNION combines the result rows of two or more SELECT statements and removes duplicate rows from the combined result
To permanently change the database schema
To disable query filtering
To create a new database connection
questions.answer: UNION combines the result rows of two or more SELECT statements and removes duplicate rows from the combined result
questions.explanation: This describes the central operation taught in this lesson.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the sample queries is correct?
options: The query result depends on the input rows and the SQL condition
SQL always returns rows in insertion order
Aliases permanently rename source columns
A SELECT query always changes stored data
questions.answer: The query result depends on the input rows and the SQL condition
questions.explanation: SQL result sets are determined by the selected source rows and query expressions.

questions.prompt: Why should an SQL learner inspect expected output?
options: To verify the query's meaning against actual sample data
To make every query return the same rows
To avoid using a WHERE clause
To force a database-specific syntax
questions.answer: To verify the query's meaning against actual sample data
questions.explanation: Expected output helps detect misunderstandings about filtering, grouping, duplicates or comparisons.

options: Use explicit conditions and test edge cases
Omit conditions to shorten every query
Assume NULL behaves like zero
Rely on unspecified row order
questions.answer: Use explicit conditions and test edge cases
questions.explanation: Explicit query logic and edge-case testing make results easier to reason about.

questions.prompt: What should be done when a feature differs between database engines?
options: Label the dialect and verify the target engine's support
Assume all SQL engines behave identically
Remove the compatibility note
Silently replace the syntax without explanation
questions.answer: Label the dialect and verify the target engine's support
questions.explanation: Dialect-aware teaching avoids promising features that the learner's runtime cannot execute.
